Force and pressure:
Pressure is the force that acts perpendicular to a surface divided by the area of that surface: P = F / A. The SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2. Weight is the force of gravity, W = m × g, with g ≈ 10 N/kg.

For the same force, a smaller area gives a larger pressure. For the same area, a larger force gives a larger pressure. Always convert areas to m^2 before calculating.
Pressure in solids:
A solid object at rest presses on a surface with its weight, so P = weight / contact area. A solid transmits force mainly in the direction of the push.

To increase pressure, reduce the contact area or increase the force. This is why knives, needles and nails are sharp. To decrease pressure, increase the contact area. This is why skis, snowshoes, camel feet and tank tracks are wide. The same object makes more pressure on its smallest face than on its largest face.
Pressure in liquids and Pascal's princip:
A liquid presses in all directions. Pressure caused by a liquid is P = ρ × g × h, where ρ is density, g ≈ 10 N/kg and h is depth. It increases with depth and does not depend on the container's shape. Total pressure equals atmospheric pressure plus ρ × g × h.

Pascal's principle: a pressure change in an enclosed liquid is passed on equally to every part of it. In a hydraulic lift, F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, so a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston.
Pressure in gases and air pressure:
Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of a container. Atmospheric pressure comes from the weight of the air above us. At sea level it is about 101 325 Pa, 1 atm or 76 cmHg. It acts in all directions and decreases with height. A mercury barometer measures it.

Boyle's law: for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, P1 × V1 = P2 × V2. If the volume gets smaller, the pressure gets larger.
